paragraphs.context: One day while I was writing Lions at
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer got stuck, and a letter from a reader gave her an idea.
paragraphs.simple: While writing this book, the writer did not know what should happen when the warrior catches Jack and Annie. She stopped and read letters from children. A boy named Mark said Jack and Annie could visit the tree house on the way home from the food shop. Then she had a good idea: they could make friends with the warrior.

background.term: A light bulb went on in my head
background.note: This means "I suddenly had a good idea." In cartoons, a light bulb over a head shows a new idea.
A state in the north-east of the United States.

paragraphs.context: Thank you, Mark. Thanks to all you readers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer thanks her readers.
paragraphs.simple: Thank you, Mark, and thank you to all my readers. Your love for these books helps me write more.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie were walking home from the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie are walking home with food from the shop.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie were walking home from the food shop. Jack's backpack was heavy. In it there was a big jar of peanut butter and some bread.

background.note: Peanut butter is a soft food made from peanuts. American children often eat it in sandwiches.

paragraphs.context: “Are you going to have a peanut butter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie asks what kind of sandwich Jack will make.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked: will you eat peanut butter with jelly, or peanut butter with honey?

background.note: A very popular American lunch: bread with peanut butter and sweet fruit jelly (jam).

paragraphs.context: He pointed to the edge of the Frog
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees a small animal like a deer.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pointed to the edge of the woods. In the dark under the trees there was a small, thin animal. It looked like a little deer.

paragraphs.context: “It’s a sign,” whispered Annie. “Remember when we
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks the animal is a sign.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said quietly, "It is a sign. Do you remember the rabbit? It showed us that we were going to the Wild West."

background.note: In Book 10, Jack and Annie went to the American West of long ago. A rabbit was a sign of that trip.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie didn’t stop to think. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run after the animal.
paragraphs.simple: They did not stop to think. They ran after it as fast as they could. Jack's heavy bag hit his back again and again.

paragraphs.context: There was the magic tree house. It was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The magic tree house is back in the tallest tree.
paragraphs.simple: There was the magic tree house at the top of the tallest tree. It was shining in the midday sun. Its rope ladder moved in the dark below it.

paragraphs.context: Morgan le Fay wasn’t waving at them from
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is not at the window.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan le Fay was not waving at them. She was not at the window at all.

background.note: A magic woman from the old stories of King Arthur. In these books she is a librarian, and the tree house is hers.

paragraphs.context: Sunlight streamed through the window. It lit a
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sun shines on the books and the scrolls.
paragraphs.simple: Sunlight came in through the window. It shone on a pile of books and two scrolls. The old scrolls had the answers to two riddles that Jack and Annie solved before.

paragraphs.context: Morgan le Fay had appeared out of nowhere.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is suddenly there.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan le Fay was suddenly there. No one saw her come. In the bright light she looked very old and very beautiful.

paragraphs.context: “Do you still want to become Master Librarians?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan asks if they still want to be Master Librarians.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan asked, "Do you still want to become Master Librarians and help me in my work?"

background.note: In Books 9 to 12, Morgan gives Jack and Annie four riddles. If they solve all four, they become Master Librarians and can help her.

paragraphs.context: “You’ve solved two riddles so far,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives them the third riddle.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said, "You have solved two riddles. Here is the third." She gave the scroll to Annie.

paragraphs.context: She pulled a book out from her robe
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives Jack a book about Africa.
paragraphs.simple: She took a book from her robe and gave it to Jack. On the cover it said THE PLAINS OF AFRICA.

background.note: Africa is a very big continent, south of Europe. Its plains have many wild animals, like lions, zebras and giraffes.

paragraphs.context: It showed hordes of zebras, tall giraffes, big
paragraphs.mainIdea: The picture shows many African animals.
paragraphs.simple: The picture showed very many zebras, tall giraffes, big animals with horns and small animals like deer.

paragraphs.context: “A Thomson’s gazelle, I believe,” Morgan said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan names the small animal.
paragraphs.simple: "I think it is a Thomson's gazelle," Morgan said.

background.note: A small, fast gazelle from East Africa. It has a black stripe on its side and runs at up to 80 kilometres an hour.

paragraphs.context: “Be careful,” said Morgan. “Just keep an eye
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan tells them to watch out.
paragraphs.simple: "Be careful," said Morgan. "Just watch carefully."
paragraphs.tone: Morgan does not say what to watch for. This makes us want to read on.

paragraphs.context: The wind had started to blow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wind starts to blow.
paragraphs.simple: The wind had started to blow.

paragraphs.context: Bright light flooded the tree house again. A
paragraphs.mainIdea: They arrive, and they hear a sound outside.
paragraphs.simple: Bright light filled the tree house. They heard a soft sound outside, like leaves moving.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out, too. A giraffe was eating
paragraphs.mainIdea: A giraffe is eating leaves from their tree.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked out too. A giraffe was eating leaves from the tree. It had a sweet, silly face.

paragraphs.context: Jack peered at the world beyond the giraffe.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot believe what he sees.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked carefully at the land beyond the giraffe. What he saw was hard to believe.

paragraphs.context: He saw a huge grassy plain, a wide
paragraphs.mainIdea: The plain is full of animals.
paragraphs.simple: He saw a very big flat field of grass, a wide river and very many birds and animals, more than he ever thought he could see in one place.

paragraphs.context: Giraffes and zebras were on the side of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Different animals are on the two sides of the river.
paragraphs.simple: Giraffes and zebras were on Jack and Annie's side of the river. Gazelles and the big animals with horns were on the other side.

paragraphs.context: Every year, in late spring, thousands of zebras
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the animals migrate every year.
paragraphs.simple: Every year, at the end of spring, many zebras and gazelles and millions of wildebeests travel from the dry plains of Tanzania to Kenya.

background.note: A country in East Africa. The Serengeti plain is there.
A country in East Africa, north of Tanzania. Many people go there to see wild animals.
This big trip is called the Great Migration. About two million animals walk in a big circle every year to find fresh grass and water.

paragraphs.context: Jack pushed his glasses into place. “It means
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains the word "migrate".
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushed his glasses back up. "It means they go to a different place for part of the year, like birds that fly south for the winter."

paragraphs.context: Before they are safe in Kenya, the animals
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals must cross a river.
paragraphs.simple: To get to Kenya, the animals must first cross the Mara River. Zebras go first, then wildebeests. The small gazelles swim last.

background.note: A river in Kenya and Tanzania. When the animals cross it, crocodiles wait in the water. It is very dangerous for them.

paragraphs.context: On the far side of the river, the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals are afraid to jump into the river.
paragraphs.simple: On the far side, the animals with horns stood at the top of the high river bank. They looked down at the fast water. They were afraid.

paragraphs.context: He studied the broad plain. “I wonder where
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is still thinking about lions.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at the wide plain. "Where are the lions?" he wondered.
paragraphs.tone: Jack asks about the lions again and again. This makes the reader feel worried too.

paragraphs.context: “Those wild beasts on the other side!” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to help the animals.
paragraphs.simple: "Those wild animals on the other side! I have to help them cross," said Annie.

paragraphs.context: I’m the color of gold and as sweet
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riddle.
paragraphs.simple: My color is gold and I am very sweet. But be careful of the danger all around me. What am I?
paragraphs.tone: This is a riddle. Try to guess the answer before Jack and Annie do!

paragraphs.context: But there was no stopping her. Jack watched
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie goes down into the grass.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not stop her. She jumped off the ladder and walked through the tall grass, between the zebras and giraffes.

paragraphs.context: This is okay, he thought. He just had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels fine, but he worries about one thing.
paragraphs.simple: This is all right, Jack thought. He had only one small question.

paragraphs.context: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells Jack about giraffes.
paragraphs.simple: The giraffe is the tallest animal. Its legs can be about two metres tall, and its feet can be as big as dinner plates. A giraffe can kick very hard, so it is dangerous to attack. That is why lions usually stay away from giraffes.
paragraphs.tone: Remember this fact! It is important at the end of the story.

background.note: About 1.8 metres. Americans often use feet and inches, not metres.

paragraphs.context: Zebras live in family groups. As no two
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each zebra has its own stripes.
paragraphs.simple: Zebras live in family groups. No two zebras have the same stripes. So each baby zebra must learn what its mother's stripes look like.

paragraphs.context: Jack studied the zebras, trying to see their
paragraphs.mainIdea: The stripes make Jack dizzy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tried to see the different stripes. But in the soft, unclear light, all the lines made his head feel strange.

paragraphs.context: Zebras are the first to cross the river
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals eat the grass in turns.
paragraphs.simple: Zebras cross the river first because they eat the hardest grass. They eat the top part. Then the wildebeests come and eat the next part. They make the grass ready for the gazelles, which come last.

paragraphs.context: Wow, thought Jack. Each animal depends on the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each animal needs the one before it.
paragraphs.simple: Wow, Jack thought. Each animal needs the animal that goes before it.

paragraphs.context: He put away the Africa book and his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs to the river with his heavy bag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put the book and notebook away and ran slowly to the river. His bag was heavy and full of hard bits, and it hit his back. He forgot to take out the peanut butter and the bread.

paragraphs.context: She had vanished.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is gone.
paragraphs.simple: She was gone.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Something bad has happened already.
paragraphs.simple: The trip had only just started, and already something terrible had happened!
paragraphs.tone: Short sentences in this part make the story fast and worrying.

paragraphs.context: He wove his way between the grazing zebras
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs between the animals.
paragraphs.simple: He ran in and out between the zebras and giraffes on his way to the river.

paragraphs.context: Annie had fallen into a pool of mud
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is stuck in deep mud.
paragraphs.simple: Annie had fallen into a hole of mud near the water. The thick black mud came up to her chest.

paragraphs.context: “I slipped,” she said. “It feels like quicksand.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says the mud pulls her down.
paragraphs.simple: "I slipped," she said. "It feels like sand that pulls you down."

background.note: Quicksand is very wet sand. If you step in it, you sink. It is best to move slowly and lie back.

paragraphs.context: Jack pointed to a tangle of old tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tells Annie to hold the roots.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pointed to some old tree roots coming out of the river bank. "Hold those!" he said.

paragraphs.context: “Hold on!” Jack looked around wildly. He saw
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks for something to help.
paragraphs.simple: "Hold on!" Jack looked all around quickly. He saw a fallen branch near the bank.

paragraphs.context: He raced to it, picked it up, and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is sinking deeper.
paragraphs.simple: He ran to it and brought it back to Annie. Now only her head and arms were above the mud.

paragraphs.context: On the other side of the wide river,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wildebeests start to swim toward them.
paragraphs.simple: On the other side of the river, a wildebeest jumped into the water. Then another, and another. They were swimming right toward Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.tone: The danger grows. Annie is stuck, and the animals are coming.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, Jack, on the moon it felt like
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes a joke about her weight.
paragraphs.simple: "Jack, on the moon I felt very light," said Annie. "In this mud I feel very, very heavy."
paragraphs.tone: Annie makes a joke, even in danger.

background.note: In Book 8, Jack and Annie went to the moon. Things weigh much less there, so they felt very light.

paragraphs.context: The lead wildebeests were halfway across, swimming toward
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first wildebeests are halfway across.
paragraphs.simple: The first wildebeests were in the middle of the river, swimming toward them. Many more were jumping into the water.

paragraphs.context: A huge vulture circled overhead.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A vulture flies over them.
paragraphs.simple: A very big vulture flew round and round above them.

background.note: Vultures eat dead animals. They often fly in circles over an animal that is going to die. That is why Jack says it thinks Annie is "near the end".

paragraphs.context: In a burst of fury, she let go
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie gets angry and grabs the roots.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly very angry, she let go of the branch. She jumped forward and grabbed the roots. She got them!

paragraphs.context: Slowly, Annie pulled herself out. She was covered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is out, but covered with mud.
paragraphs.simple: Slowly Annie pulled herself out. She had black mud all over her body.

paragraphs.context: “The wildebeests will get stuck in the mudhole!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is afraid the wildebeests will get stuck.
paragraphs.simple: "The wildebeests will get stuck in the mud!" she cried. She waved her arms at the animals trying to swim across.

paragraphs.context: But the frantic swimmers kept coming.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals keep coming.
paragraphs.simple: But the swimming animals were afraid, and they kept coming.

paragraphs.context: She raced down the bank, until she reached
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie runs to a safe place.
paragraphs.simple: She ran down the bank to a clear place with sand.

paragraphs.context: Jack watched in disbelief as the swimmers changed
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wildebeests follow Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not believe it. The swimming animals changed their way. Slowly they all swam to where Annie stood. She waved them in, like a policeman in a street.

paragraphs.context: They ran farther up the river, away from
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie run away from the animals.
paragraphs.simple: They ran up the river, away from the wildebeests that were coming in. Then they stopped to rest and breathe. They looked back.

paragraphs.context: Everything seemed fine. The wildebeests were scrambling safely
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wildebeests are safe.
paragraphs.simple: Everything looked fine. The wildebeests were climbing safely up the bank. Soon they would eat the grass the zebras had made ready.

paragraphs.context: High-pitched laughter rang through the air. It sounded
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hear an unkind laugh.
paragraphs.simple: They heard a very high laugh. It sounded unkind, as if someone was laughing at them.

paragraphs.context: The creatures had bodies like dogs, but with
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals look like dogs.
paragraphs.simple: The animals had bodies like dogs, but their backs went down at the end. They laughed again.

paragraphs.context: On the African plains, the hyena (hi-EE-nuh) is
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells Jack about hyenas.
paragraphs.simple: On the African plains, the hyena is the strongest hunter after the lion. Its call sounds like a high human laugh.

background.note: Say hi-EE-nuh. Spotted hyenas live in groups. People think they only steal food, but they are very good hunters too.

paragraphs.context: The hyena has a reputation for being a
paragraphs.mainIdea: People say bad things about hyenas.
paragraphs.simple: People think the hyena is a thief and is not brave.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie made terrible monster faces. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie try to scare the hyenas.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie made terrible monster faces. They put their hands out and ran at the hyenas.

paragraphs.context: The hyenas yelped and scurried off.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hyenas run away.
paragraphs.simple: The hyenas gave a short, high cry and ran off.

paragraphs.context: She pointed to the edge of the forest.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a pond.
paragraphs.simple: She pointed to the edge of the forest. There was a small pond with tall grass all around it. Zebras were drinking there.

paragraphs.context: When they reached the edge of the water,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hears something.
paragraphs.simple: At the water, Jack put his heavy bag down in the dry grass. He looked around. He could see no lions. But then he heard something.

paragraphs.context: On the far side of the pond, something
paragraphs.mainIdea: Something big comes out of the trees.
paragraphs.simple: On the other side of the pond, something very big was coming out of the trees.
paragraphs.tone: The chapter stops here, so we want to know what it is.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stood frozen as an elephant
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is an elephant.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie did not move. An elephant came out of the dark. It walked into the pond and put its trunk into the water.

paragraphs.context: Jack breathed a sigh of relief. An elephant
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is happy it is an elephant, not a lion.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed out. He felt better. An elephant was not going to run after them and eat them. But it was still very big.

paragraphs.context: “Fine,” said Jack. He was tired of Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is tired of Annie and wants to go alone.
paragraphs.simple: "Fine," said Jack. He did not like it when Annie stopped to do other things. "I will solve the riddle alone. See you at the tree house."

paragraphs.context: He turned to go. A spray of water
paragraphs.mainIdea: Water falls on Jack.
paragraphs.simple: He turned to go. Water came down on him from behind. He shouted and looked back.

paragraphs.context: The elephant sprayed her again … then again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elephant washes Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The elephant sprayed her again and again. The mud slowly came off her face, her hair, her clothes, her legs and her shoes.

paragraphs.context: Jack stepped forward and shut his eyes tight.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elephant washes Jack too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stepped forward and closed his eyes hard. A strong rush of water hit him. It felt like a very strong shower.

paragraphs.context: He picked up his heavy pack. “We have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to solve the riddle and go.
paragraphs.simple: He picked up his heavy bag. "We must find the answer to the riddle, so we can leave before we meet real trouble."

paragraphs.context: The bird twittered and flew around Jack and
paragraphs.mainIdea: A little gray bird flies around them.
paragraphs.simple: The bird made small, high sounds and flew around them. Its feathers were a plain gray, but it seemed bright and happy.

paragraphs.context: Jack let out a long sigh. “You are
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is tired of Annie today.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed out for a long time. "You are making me very tired today," he said.

paragraphs.context: The bird darted toward the trees. It landed
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird wants them to follow.
paragraphs.simple: The bird flew quickly to the trees. It sat on a branch and turned its head to one side as it looked at them.

paragraphs.context: The forest was cooler than the sunny plains.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The forest is cool and dark.
paragraphs.simple: The forest was cooler than the sunny plains. It was full of shadows and the calls of birds.

paragraphs.context: Bright rays streamed between the trees. Green leaves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sunlight comes in between the trees.
paragraphs.simple: Lines of bright sunlight came in between the trees. Leaves and plants moved in the light, which had little spots of sun and shade.

paragraphs.context: “Yuck, what’s that?” said Annie. She pointed at
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie sees a strange brown thing with bees.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed at a round brown thing hanging from a low branch. Bees were flying around it.

paragraphs.context: But the little bird darted at the beehive
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird pecks at the beehive.
paragraphs.simple: But the little bird flew at the beehive and hit it with its beak.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his Africa book. He kept turning
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the bird will not be in the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack kept turning the pages. As he thought, there was no gray bird in the book.

paragraphs.context: Jack turned one more page. And there it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird is in the book after all.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turned one more page. There it was: a little gray bird, a beehive and a tall warrior with a painted face and a spear.

paragraphs.context: This bird is called a honey guide. It’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells them about the honey guide and the Masai.
paragraphs.simple: This bird is called a honey guide. It is a friend and helper of the Masai people. The Masai are an African tribe. People know them as strong, brave fighters.

background.note: Say muh-SI (also spelled Maasai). The Masai people live in Kenya and Tanzania. Many keep cows and wear bright red clothes.
This is a real bird. People in Africa really follow it to beehives, and it eats the wax that is left.

paragraphs.context: The honey guide leads a Masai tribesperson to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird and people work together.
paragraphs.simple: The honey guide takes a Masai person to a beehive. It waits for the person to make the bees fly away and take the honey. Then the bird eats the honeycomb.

paragraphs.context: “That’s cool,” said Jack. “They work together, like
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals and the bird all work together.
paragraphs.simple: "That's great," said Jack. "They work together, like the zebras, wildebeests and gazelles."
paragraphs.tone: This is a big idea in the book: animals and people need each other.

paragraphs.context: Jack put his book and backpack down. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: They make the bees go away.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his book and bag down. He and Annie pulled up the plants and waved them near the tree. The bees flew away.

paragraphs.context: Next, Jack grabbed the tree branch and jiggled
paragraphs.mainIdea: The beehive falls and breaks.
paragraphs.simple: Then Jack held the branch and moved it quickly up and down. The hive fell to the ground and broke.

paragraphs.context: Jack stuck his finger in the honeycomb, too.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tastes the honey.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his finger in too. He licked off the honey. It was the sweetest honey he ever tasted.

paragraphs.context: “It’s weird,” said Annie. “Honey’s so sweet and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says something important about honey.
paragraphs.simple: "Honey is so sweet and good. But to get it, you must go past many dangerous bees."
paragraphs.tone: Annie does not know it, but she has just said the answer to the riddle.

paragraphs.context: Standing in the shadows was a tall man
paragraphs.mainIdea: A Masai warrior is standing there.
paragraphs.simple: In the shadows stood a tall man. He had a spear and a curved sword on his belt. His face was painted in strong, bright colors.

paragraphs.context: “We didn’t mean to steal anything,” Jack said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says they did not want to steal.
paragraphs.simple: "We did not want to steal anything," said Jack. "Really, it is all yours. We have had enough."

paragraphs.context: The warrior narrowed his eyes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior looks hard at them.
paragraphs.simple: The warrior made his eyes small, as if he was thinking hard.

paragraphs.context: “I’m sorry we were trespassing,” said Jack. “We
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack offers the warrior a gift.
paragraphs.simple: "I am sorry we came onto your land," said Jack. "We come as friends. We even have presents." He held his bag out to the warrior.

paragraphs.context: “Peanut butter!” He pulled out the loaf of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack has an idea: a sandwich.
paragraphs.simple: "Peanut butter! Bread! How about a peanut butter and honey sandwich?"
paragraphs.tone: Now we see the idea from the writer's letter: Jack makes friends with food.

paragraphs.context: She spread the peanut butter onto a slice
paragraphs.mainIdea: They make a sandwich.
paragraphs.simple: Annie put peanut butter on a piece of bread with her fingers. Jack put honey on another piece.

paragraphs.context: The warrior took the sandwich, but he didn’t
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior does not eat it.
paragraphs.simple: The warrior took the sandwich but did not eat it. He just looked at it.

paragraphs.context: Finally, the warrior bit into his sandwich. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior eats the sandwich.
paragraphs.simple: At last, the warrior bit into his sandwich. He ate it slowly.

paragraphs.context: The warrior smiled. He had a kind, dignified
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior smiles.
paragraphs.simple: The warrior smiled. He had a kind, calm smile that made you respect him.

paragraphs.context: Then the warrior turned gracefully and vanished into
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior goes away.
paragraphs.simple: Then the warrior turned in a smooth, beautiful way and was gone into the trees.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” said Jack. Part of him wanted
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack would like to go with the warrior.
paragraphs.simple: "Oh, man," said Jack. Part of him wanted to follow the quiet warrior through the dark forest.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack. He put away the peanut
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants no more adventures.
paragraphs.simple: "We are going back to the tree house, right? We are not going to do silly things, like save animals or run after birds. Right?"

paragraphs.context: “Those things aren’t silly,” said Annie. “Don’t forget
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says helping is not silly.
paragraphs.simple: "Those things are not silly," said Annie. "Remember, the bird gave us the answer to the riddle."
paragraphs.tone: Annie is right. Helping others helped them too.

paragraphs.context: When they passed the pond, they saw the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elephant waves goodbye.
paragraphs.simple: When they walked past the pond, the elephant was still playing in the water. He lifted his trunk. It looked like he was waving at them.

paragraphs.context: And they saw a bunch of lions sleeping
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lions are under the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: And they saw a group of lions sleeping in the shade of a tree. It was the tree with the tree house!

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart gave a jump.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is suddenly afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's heart jumped.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie crouched in the tall grass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie hide and look at the lions.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie got down low in the tall grass. There was a big lion, three female lions and many baby lions.

paragraphs.context: After a pride of lions has eaten, they
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lions rest after they eat.
paragraphs.simple: After a group of lions has eaten, they rest for a few hours.

paragraphs.context: Sensing that the lions are not hunting at
paragraphs.mainIdea: The other animals know the lions are not hunting.
paragraphs.simple: The other animals can feel that the lions are not hunting now, so they eat grass near them.

paragraphs.context: He peered around. The words in the book
paragraphs.mainIdea: The zebras and giraffes are not worried.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked around. The book was right: the zebras and giraffes did not seem worried about the lions.

paragraphs.context: “That could take hours,” said Jack. “Plus they
paragraphs.mainIdea: Waiting is not a good idea.
paragraphs.simple: "That could take hours," said Jack. "And they might be hungry again by then."

paragraphs.context: The big lion stirred lazily. He opened his
paragraphs.mainIdea: The big lion wakes up.
paragraphs.simple: The big lion moved slowly, as if he did not want to get up. He opened his golden eyes.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt the hair rise on the back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is very afraid but does not move.
paragraphs.simple: Jack felt the hair stand up on the back of his neck. But he did not move at all.

paragraphs.context: The lion lifted his head and yawned. His
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lion yawns and looks around.
paragraphs.simple: The lion lifted his head and opened his mouth wide. His big teeth shone in the sun. He turned his head and looked around in a tired way.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath as the lion’s gaze
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lion looks at Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stopped breathing when the lion looked at him. The lion sat up. His sharp yellow eyes looked into Jack's eyes.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart raced. His mind raced. He remembered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers a fact from the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's heart beat fast. He thought fast. He remembered something from the book: lions stay away from giraffes.
paragraphs.tone: This is the fact from Chapter 3. Reading helps Jack save them!

paragraphs.context: The giraffe’s legs were so long, Jack and
paragraphs.mainIdea: They stand under the giraffe.
paragraphs.simple: The giraffe's legs were very long, so Jack and Annie could stand up under it. Jack's head only just touched its golden stomach.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked in the same rhythm
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk with the giraffe.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie walked in step with the giraffe.

paragraphs.context: They got closer and closer to the tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: They get closer to the tree house and the lions.
paragraphs.simple: They got nearer and nearer to the tree house, and nearer and nearer to the lions.

paragraphs.context: When the rope ladder was just a few
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run to the ladder.
paragraphs.simple: When the ladder was only a few steps away, they ran out from under the giraffe to the ladder.

paragraphs.context: As they climbed, the lion growled and leaped
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lion jumps at the ladder.
paragraphs.simple: As they climbed, the lion made an angry sound and jumped at the ladder.

paragraphs.context: Annie had already unrolled the scroll. The riddle
paragraphs.mainIdea: The answer is on the scroll.
paragraphs.simple: Annie had already opened the scroll. The riddle was gone. Now there was only one shining word on it.

paragraphs.context: Jack grabbed the Pennsylvania book. He opened it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack makes a wish to go home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took the Pennsylvania book. He opened it at the picture of the Frog Creek woods.

background.note: A state in the east of the United States. Jack and Annie's town, Frog Creek, is there.

paragraphs.context: “Iwishwecouldgothere!” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the wish very fast.
paragraphs.simple: "I wish we could go there!" he said, so fast that the words ran together.
paragraphs.tone: The words are joined to show how fast and afraid Jack is.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. His heart was still
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are home, but Jack is still afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. His heart was still beating fast. He could still hear the hyenas laughing in his mind.

paragraphs.context: “The giraffe was the true honey on that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says the giraffe was the real honey.
paragraphs.simple: "The giraffe was the real honey on this trip," she said. "It was sweet and golden, and there was danger all around it."

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” Jack said. “And now we have just
paragraphs.mainIdea: They have one more riddle.
paragraphs.simple: "Yes," said Jack. "Now we have only one more riddle."

background.note: The fourth riddle is in the next book, Polar Bears Past Bedtime.

paragraphs.context: “Oh … just say we had a picnic
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack makes a joke about what to tell Mom.
paragraphs.simple: "Just say we had a picnic with a Masai warrior in Africa," said Jack.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is joking. Mom would never believe the true story.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack, “and after you fell into
paragraphs.mainIdea: They remember the whole adventure.
paragraphs.simple: "And after you fell into a mud hole because you were helping a million wildebeests cross a river."
paragraphs.tone: They tell the story backward, from the end to the start. It is a funny way to remember everything.

paragraphs.context: Then Jack pushed his glasses into place. “We
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack decides to tell Mom something simple.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushed his glasses up. "We should just say we ate our sandwiches on the way home from the store."

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack, “with, like—ten chapters.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack makes a joke about the story.
paragraphs.simple: "Right," said Jack, "a story with about ten chapters."
paragraphs.tone: This is a joke: this book has ten chapters!

sentences.context: He had written to suggest that Jack and Annie decide to visit the tree house on their way home from the grocery store.
sentences.simple: He wrote to give an idea: Jack and Annie could go to the tree house while they were walking home from the food shop.

parts.meaning: "So that you can help me?"

sentences.context: He saw a huge grassy plain, a wide river, and tons of birds and animals—more than he had ever imagined in one place.
sentences.simple: He saw a big flat field of grass, a wide river and very many birds and animals. There were more than he ever thought he could see in one place.

sentences.grammar: Look for the list with commas and "and". The long line (—) adds an idea. "Tons of" is a friendly way to say "very many".

parts.text: because they eat the coarsest grass.
parts.meaning: because they eat the hardest grass.

sentences.grammar: "The first to do something" means "the one who does it first".

sentences.context: His pack was heavy and lumpy, bumping against his back.
sentences.simple: His bag was heavy and full of hard bits. It kept hitting his back.
sentences.main: His pack was heavy and lumpy.

parts.text: His pack was heavy and lumpy,
parts.meaning: His bag was heavy and not smooth,

parts.text: bumping against his back.
parts.job: What the bag was doing at the same time.
parts.meaning: and it kept hitting his back.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part tells you what was happening at the same time.

sentences.context: Their trip had barely begun, and already disaster had struck!
sentences.simple: The trip had only just started, and something terrible had already happened!
sentences.main: Disaster had struck.

parts.text: Their trip had barely begun,
parts.meaning: The trip had only just started,

parts.text: and already disaster had struck!
parts.meaning: and something very bad had already happened!

sentences.grammar: "Had begun" and "had struck" both happened before this moment in the story. "Disaster struck" means "something terrible happened".

sentences.context: He raced to it, picked it up, and carried it back to Annie.
sentences.simple: He ran fast to the branch, picked it up and took it back to Annie.
sentences.main: He raced, picked it up, and carried it.

parts.text: He raced to it,
parts.meaning: He ran fast to the branch,

parts.text: picked it up,
parts.meaning: lifted it,

parts.text: and carried it back to Annie.
parts.meaning: and took it to Annie.

sentences.grammar: Three actions, one after another, with one subject "He". The commas and "and" join them.

sentences.context: “Hey, Jack, on the moon it felt like I weighed ten pounds,” said Annie. “And in this mud it feels like I weigh a ton.”
sentences.simple: Annie said, "On the moon I felt very light. In this mud I feel very, very heavy."
sentences.main: It feels like I weigh a ton.

parts.text: “Hey, Jack, on the moon it felt like I weighed ten pounds,”
parts.meaning: "On the moon I felt very light,"

parts.text: said Annie.
parts.meaning: said Annie.

parts.text: “And in this mud it feels like I weigh a ton.”
parts.meaning: "In this mud I feel very heavy."

sentences.grammar: "It felt like" (past) and "it feels like" (now) compare then and now. "Weigh a ton" means be very heavy.

sentences.context: In a burst of fury, she let go of the branch.
sentences.simple: Suddenly she was very angry, and she stopped holding the branch.
sentences.main: She let go of the branch.

parts.text: In a burst of fury,
parts.meaning: Suddenly very angry,

parts.text: she let go of the branch.
parts.meaning: she stopped holding the branch.

sentences.grammar: "In a burst of ..." means a sudden, short time of a strong feeling.

sentences.context: Jack watched in disbelief as the swimmers changed their course.
sentences.simple: Jack watched. He could not believe it: the swimming animals changed the way they were going.
sentences.main: Jack watched.

parts.text: Jack watched in disbelief
parts.meaning: Jack watched and could not believe his eyes

parts.text: as the swimmers changed their course.
parts.meaning: while the swimming animals turned a new way.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "at the same time as". "The swimmers" means the wildebeests in the water.

sentences.context: On the African plains, the hyena (hi-EE-nuh) is the ruling predator after the lion.
sentences.simple: On the African plains, only the lion is a stronger hunter than the hyena.
sentences.main: The hyena is the ruling predator.

parts.text: On the African plains,
parts.meaning: In the flat grasslands of Africa,

parts.text: the hyena (hi-EE-nuh)
parts.job: Who. The part in ( ) tells you how to say it.
parts.meaning: the hyena

parts.text: is the ruling predator
parts.meaning: is the strongest hunter

parts.text: after the lion.
parts.job: With one more: the lion is first.
parts.meaning: after the lion.

sentences.grammar: "The ruling predator after the lion" means number two. The lion is number one.

sentences.context: An elephant wasn’t going to chase them and eat them. Still, the elephant was huge.
sentences.simple: An elephant would not run after them and eat them. But it was still very big.
sentences.main: The elephant was huge.

parts.text: An elephant wasn’t going to chase them and eat them.
parts.meaning: An elephant would not run after them and eat them.

parts.text: Still, the elephant was huge.
parts.job: Second idea: but... "Still," means "But even so".
parts.meaning: But it was very big all the same.

sentences.grammar: "Still," at the start of a sentence means "but even so". It is not the same as "still" meaning "not moving".

sentences.context: So we can leave this place … before we run into real trouble.
sentences.simple: Then we can leave before something really bad happens to us.
sentences.main: We can leave this place.

parts.text: So we can leave this place …
parts.meaning: Then we can go away from here

parts.text: before we run into real trouble.
parts.meaning: before we meet real danger.

sentences.grammar: "Run into trouble" means to meet trouble you did not expect.

sentences.context: It’s both a friend and a helper to the Masai (muh-SI) people, an African tribe known for their fierce fighting skills and bravery.
sentences.simple: The bird is a friend and a helper of the Masai. The Masai are an African tribe. People know they are strong fighters and very brave.
sentences.main: It's a friend and a helper.

parts.text: It’s both a friend and a helper
parts.job: Main part. "Both ... and ..." joins two things.
parts.meaning: The bird is a friend and also a helper

parts.text: to the Masai (muh-SI) people,
parts.meaning: of the Masai people.

parts.text: an African tribe known for their fierce fighting skills and bravery.
parts.meaning: They are an African tribe. People know them for their strong fighting and brave hearts.

sentences.grammar: After the comma, "an African tribe ..." tells you who the Masai are. "Known for" means "famous because of".

sentences.context: The bird waits for him or her to scatter the bees and take the honey.
sentences.simple: The bird waits. The person makes the bees fly away and takes the honey.
sentences.main: The bird waits.

parts.text: The bird waits
parts.meaning: The bird waits

parts.text: for him or her
parts.meaning: for the person

parts.text: to scatter the bees and take the honey.
parts.meaning: to make the bees go away and take the honey.

sentences.grammar: "Wait for someone to do something" means you wait until they do it.

sentences.context: Honey’s so sweet and good. But to get it, you have to go past a lot of dangerous bees.
sentences.simple: Honey is very sweet and good. But you must go past many dangerous bees to get it.
sentences.main: You have to go past dangerous bees.

parts.text: Honey’s so sweet and good.
parts.meaning: Honey is very sweet and good.

parts.text: But to get it,
parts.meaning: But if you want honey,

parts.text: you have to go past a lot of dangerous bees.
parts.meaning: you must go past many bees that can hurt you.

sentences.grammar: "To get it" at the start tells the goal. "Have to" means "must".

sentences.context: Standing in the shadows was a tall man with a spear and a curved sword hanging from his belt.
sentences.simple: A tall man was standing in the dark. He had a spear, and a curved sword hung from his belt.
sentences.main: A tall man was standing in the shadows.

parts.text: Standing in the shadows
parts.job: Where and what he was doing. It comes first for surprise.
parts.meaning: In the dark place,

parts.text: was a tall man
parts.job: Main part: the subject comes after the verb.
parts.meaning: there was a tall man

parts.text: with a spear and a curved sword hanging from his belt.
parts.meaning: who had a spear and a curved sword on his belt.

sentences.grammar: The usual order is "A tall man was standing in the shadows." The writer turns it round so we see the shadows first and the man last, like Jack does.

sentences.context: “We didn’t mean to steal anything,” Jack said. “In fact, it’s all yours. We’ve had enough.”
sentences.simple: Jack said, "We did not want to steal. Really, all of it is yours. We do not need more."
sentences.main: We didn't mean to steal anything.

parts.text: “We didn’t mean to steal anything,”
parts.job: First idea. "Mean to" means "want to; do on purpose".
parts.meaning: "We did not want to steal,"

parts.text: Jack said.
parts.meaning: Jack said.

parts.text: “In fact, it’s all yours. We’ve had enough.”
parts.meaning: "Really, it is all yours. We have eaten enough."

sentences.grammar: "Didn't mean to" is a polite way to say sorry: "It was not on purpose."

sentences.context: As Jack unwrapped the bread, his hands shook.
sentences.simple: Jack's hands were shaking while he opened the bread bag.
sentences.main: His hands shook.

parts.text: As Jack unwrapped the bread,
parts.meaning: While Jack took the bread out of its bag,

parts.text: his hands shook.
parts.meaning: his hands were shaking.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "while". His hands shake because he is afraid of the warrior.

sentences.context: Sensing that the lions are not hunting at the moment, the other animals graze nearby.
sentences.simple: The other animals feel that the lions are not hunting now, so they eat grass near them.
sentences.main: The other animals graze nearby.

parts.text: Sensing that the lions are not hunting at the moment,
parts.job: Why. The "-ing" part tells you what they feel.
parts.meaning: Because they feel the lions are not hunting now,

parts.text: the other animals graze nearby.
parts.meaning: the other animals eat grass close by.

sentences.grammar: A sentence can start with an "-ing" part. It tells you why or how. The main part comes after the comma.

sentences.context: Jack held his breath as the lion’s gaze rested on him.
sentences.simple: Jack stopped breathing when the lion looked at him and kept looking.
sentences.main: Jack held his breath.

parts.text: Jack held his breath
parts.meaning: Jack stopped breathing for a moment

parts.text: as the lion’s gaze rested on him.
parts.meaning: while the lion looked at him and did not look away.

sentences.grammar: "Gaze" is a long look. When a look "rests on" you, it stops on you.

sentences.context: The giraffe’s legs were so long, Jack and Annie could stand up under it.
sentences.simple: The giraffe's legs were very long. So Jack and Annie could stand up under it.
sentences.main: The giraffe's legs were so long.

parts.text: The giraffe’s legs were so long,
parts.meaning: The giraffe's legs were very, very long,

parts.text: Jack and Annie could stand up under it.
parts.meaning: so the children could stand under it.

sentences.grammar: "So ... (that) ..." shows a result: the legs were very long, and because of that they could stand under it. "That" is left out here.

sentences.context: They got closer and closer to the tree house—and closer and closer to the pride of lions.
sentences.simple: They got nearer and nearer to the tree house. But that also meant nearer and nearer to the lions.
sentences.main: They got closer and closer.

parts.text: They got closer and closer to the tree house
parts.meaning: They came nearer and nearer to the tree house

parts.text: —and closer and closer to the pride of lions.
parts.meaning: and also nearer and nearer to the group of lions.

sentences.grammar: "Closer and closer" means getting more and more close. The writer says it twice to show good news and bad news at the same time.

sentences.context: “Right,” said Jack, “and after you fell into a mudhole because you were helping a million wildebeests migrate across a river.”
sentences.simple: Jack said, "Yes, and that was after you fell into the mud, because you were helping very many wildebeests cross a river."
sentences.main: You fell into a mudhole.

parts.text: “Right,” said Jack,
parts.meaning: "Yes," said Jack,

parts.text: “and after you fell into a mudhole
parts.meaning: "and that was after you fell into the mud

parts.text: because you were helping a million wildebeests migrate across a river.”
parts.meaning: because you were helping very many animals travel across a river."

sentences.grammar: "Help someone do something": after "help" you can use a verb with no "to": "helping wildebeests migrate".

a sigh of relief.meaning: A long breath out when you feel happy that something bad did not happen.
a sigh of relief.example: Jack breathed a sigh of relief.
a sigh of relief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

according to.example: According to the riddle, we’re looking for something gold and sweet.
according to.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

are you kidding.meaning: Are you joking? You say it when something seems silly or hard to believe.
are you kidding.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

at once.example: Jack knew at once what he was.
at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

at the moment.example: the lions are not hunting at the moment
at the moment.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

beat it.meaning: Go away! (said in a rude, angry way)

break in.meaning: To start talking when someone else is talking.
break in.example: “What did they have for lunch?” Annie broke in.
break in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

break open.meaning: To break so that the inside can be seen.
break open.example: The hive fell to the ground and broke open.
break open.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

calm down.meaning: To stop being worried or excited and become quiet again.
calm down.example: Jack took another moment to calm down.
calm down.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

catch one's breath.meaning: To stop and rest until you can breathe normally again after running.
catch one's breath.example: they stopped to catch their breath
catch one's breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

come in peace.meaning: To come as a friend, not to fight.

drive someone crazy.meaning: To make someone very angry or tired.
drive someone crazy.example: You are driving me crazy today
drive someone crazy.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

dry off.meaning: To become dry, or to make someone dry.
dry off.example: When the sun dries me off, I’ll be like new.
dry off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

faster and faster.example: The tree house spun faster and faster.
faster and faster.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it or find the answer.
figure out.example: I couldn’t figure out what should happen
figure out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

from head to toe.example: She was covered with the black mud from head to toe.
from head to toe.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

get on one's knees.meaning: To go down so your knees are on the ground.
get on one's knees.example: Jack threw down his pack and got on his knees.

get out of here.meaning: Go away! (said in an angry or excited way)
get out of here.example: “Oh, get out of here!” Annie shouted at the vulture.
get out of here.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

give a jump.meaning: To move suddenly because of surprise or fear. "His heart gave a jump" means he was suddenly afraid.

go ahead.meaning: You say it to tell someone they can start doing something.
go ahead.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

had better.meaning: Should; must, or something bad may happen. "She'd better hurry" means she should hurry.
had better.example: I’d better stop her before there’s trouble
had better.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

hold on.meaning: 1. To hold something tightly so you do not fall. 2. Wait!
hold on.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

hold one's breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, because you are afraid or excited.
hold one's breath.example: Jack held his breath as the lion’s gaze rested on him.
hold one's breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand forward with something in it, so someone can take it.
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

hold up.meaning: To lift something so people can see it.
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

honey guide.meaning: A small African bird that leads people to beehives. Then it eats the honeycomb.
honey guide.example: This bird is called a honey guide.

how about.meaning: Would you like...? You say it to offer something or give an idea.
how about.example: How about a peanut butter and honey sandwich?
how about.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

in disbelief.meaning: Not able to believe what you see or hear.
in disbelief.example: Jack watched in disbelief as the swimmers changed their course.
in disbelief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in fact.meaning: Really; you say it to add something true or surprising.
in fact.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

in its place.meaning: Where it was before; instead of it.
in its place.example: In its place was one shimmering word
in its place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in sight.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in silence.meaning: Without talking or making a sound.
in silence.example: They ate their sandwiches in silence.
in silence.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in the distance.example: they saw the wildebeests in the distance
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

keep an eye out.meaning: To watch carefully for something, often something dangerous.
keep an eye out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

keep it up.meaning: Keep doing it! You are doing well.
keep it up.example: “Keep it up,” she shouted to the wildebeests
keep it up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

let go of.example: she let go of the branch
let go of.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, like a sigh or a cry.
let out.example: the elephant let out a grunt
let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

like new.meaning: As good as new; looking new again.
like new.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

look around.meaning: To turn your head and look at the things around you.
look around.example: Finally, they stopped and looked around.
look around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

look her up.meaning: To find her name in a book and read about her.
look her up.example: Look her up in the book
look her up.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

look like.meaning: To seem to be something, because of how it looks.
look like.example: It looked like a tiny deer.
look like.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

look up.meaning: To raise your eyes and look at something above you.
look up.example: Just then, a shadow passed over them. Jack looked up.
look up.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

make friends with.meaning: To start to be friends with someone.
make friends with.example: a way Jack and Annie could make friends with the warrior
make friends with.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

now or never.meaning: We must do it now. There will be no other chance.
now or never.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

of course.meaning: Surely; yes. You say it when something is easy to know.
of course.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

on the way home.example: on their way home from the grocery store
on the way home.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

out of nowhere.meaning: Suddenly, when no one saw it coming.
out of nowhere.example: Morgan le Fay had appeared out of nowhere.
out of nowhere.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

peanut butter.meaning: A soft brown food made from crushed peanuts. You spread it on bread.
peanut butter.example: It held a big jar of peanut butter and a loaf of bread.
peanut butter.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pick up.meaning: To take something in your hand and lift it.
pick up.example: He picked up the book on Africa
pick up.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place, for example in a bag.
put away.example: He put away the Africa book and his notebook.
put away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

put out.meaning: To move your hands forward, away from your body.
put out.example: They put out their hands and rushed at the hyenas.

run into.meaning: To meet something or someone you did not expect, often trouble.
run into.example: before we run into real trouble
run into.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

same here.meaning: Me too; it is the same for me.
same here.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

scare off.meaning: To make someone or something afraid so they run away.
scare off.example: And we scared off two hyenas.
scare off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

see ya.meaning: Goodbye. ("Ya" is a friendly way to say "you".)

take a bite.meaning: To bite off a small piece of food.
take a bite.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

take a break.meaning: To stop working for a short time and rest.
take a break.example: I decided to take a break and read some letters
take a break.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often before doing something hard.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: 1. To take a bag or clothes off your body. 2. To run away quickly.
take off.example: Jack took off his heavy pack.
take off.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

take out.meaning: To pull something out of a bag or a box.
take out.example: He’d forgotten to take out the jar of peanut butter
take out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

too late.meaning: After the right time; when it is not possible any more.
too late.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.
